etymology: Latin numerus (number) + Greek logos (word, account) — literally “the account of number.” In the MOOP Dictionary the word names two opposite things that must never be confused: the biblical symbolism of number, and the occult manipulation of number.
biblical_def: Scripture is not indifferent to number. God “telleth the number of the stars” and numbers His people; He orders creation in six days and rests the seventh; He seals twelve tribes and twelve apostles; He tests in forties and completes in sevens. This patterned use of number is real, authorial, and typological—it arises from the text itself and from the God who counts, weighs, and measures all things. To read it rightly is simply to read Scripture attentively: seven speaks of completion, six of man and his labor under the sun, eight of new beginning and resurrection, twelve of the covenant people, forty of testing and probation. Biblical numerology, so understood, is a servant of exegesis. It is sharply distinguished, however, from occult numerology—gematria worked as divination, the hunt for hidden codes, “angel numbers,” and every attempt to wring secret knowledge or luck from figures. Deuteronomy forbids divination; Scripture never invites the reader to decode it as a cipher but to believe and obey it as the Word of God. The number is a signpost, not an oracle.
webster_summary: The study of the theological and typological significance of numbers as God actually uses them in Scripture—to be received as an aid to reading the text, never as a system of divination.
webster_full: NUMEROLOGY, n. In its lawful and biblical sense, the disciplined observation that God employs number meaningfully in His Word: seven for completion, twelve for the covenant people, forty for probation, and the like. So used, it is a branch of careful reading, always subordinate to the plain sense of the text.

In its corrupt sense, the occult art of assigning hidden powers to numbers—gematria as divination, lucky and unlucky figures, “angel numbers,” and New Age systems that promise secret knowledge. Scripture condemns all divination; number in the Bible reveals God’s order, it does not conceal a code for the initiated.

Here is wisdom. Let him that hath understanding count the number of the beast: for it is the number of a man; and his number is Six hundred threescore and six.
Psalm 90:12
So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
Genesis 1:14
And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of the heaven to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years: the
Proverbs 9:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
corruption_summary: Modern culture severs number from the God who orders it—turning biblical symbolism either into occult divination (gematria, “angel numbers”) or into mere superstition (lucky sevens, dreaded thirteens).
corruption_paragraphs: The occult corruption treats number as a hidden power to be manipulated: Kabbalistic gematria worked for secret meanings, New Age “angel numbers” read off a clock, numerology charts that claim to reveal destiny from a birth date. This is precisely the divination Scripture forbids—an attempt to gain knowledge and control apart from God’s revealed Word.

The superstitious corruption is the same error in a secular coat: lucky numbers, fear of the thirteenth floor, the dread of 666 detached from its actual meaning in Revelation. Both corruptions forget that biblical number is not magic but meaning—the ordered speech of the God who made and numbers all things.
roots_summary: From Latin numerus and Greek logos; the biblical usage descends from the Hebrew Scriptures’ own patterned counting rather than from pagan number-magic.
roots_lines: Latin numerus — number, a counting.
Greek logos — word, account, reasoned discourse.
Hebrew saphar ('to count, recount, declare') — the root behind both numbering and the sepher (book): to count is to tell.
Contrast: qesem (divination) — the forbidden counterfeit that reads figures for hidden fate.
usage: Sound biblical numerology notes that Christ rose on the eighth day—the first day of a new creation—without turning the observation into a code.
She abandoned her numerology app when she saw it was simply divination dressed in spiritual language.
The elder warned that hunting Revelation for hidden numeric dates is occult numerology, not the sober reading the text commands.

etymology: Old English an; the cardinal of unity. In Scripture the number of God’s own oneness (echad) and of the union He makes—of husband and wife, and of Christ and His body.
biblical_def: One is the number of God. The great confession of Israel, the Shema, declares “the LORD our God, the LORD is one”—not a solitary monad but the one living and true God who eternally subsists in three Persons, undivided in essence. From this oneness flows every biblical unity. God makes of husband and wife “one flesh,” a covenant union that images His own faithfulness. Christ prays that His people “may be one, as We are one,” and the apostle grounds the church’s unity in it: “one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.” One is therefore never the number of proud isolation but of covenant communion—a unity given by God, not manufactured by men. It rebukes both the idolatry of the many gods and the individualism that would live to itself. To confess one God is to be bound into one people; the number that begins all counting is the number that gathers the redeemed into one.
webster_summary: The number of unity: first, the oneness of the one true God; then the covenant unions He creates—one flesh in marriage, one body in the church.
webster_full: ONE, adj. Single in number; the first of the cardinals. In Scripture pre-eminently the number of God’s essential oneness, confessed in the Shema and never at odds with the Tri-unity of Persons.

ONE, n. The unity God creates and commands: the one-flesh bond of marriage, the one body of the church, the one faith once delivered. Biblical oneness is covenantal communion, not the lonely self-sufficiency the modern age prizes.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 6:4
Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD:

Ephesians 4:4
There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling;
corruption_summary: Modernity keeps the word one but empties it of covenant—turning it into the autonomous individual (“be your one true self”) rather than the God-given union of the Shema and the one-flesh bond.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption is individualism: the “number one” as the sovereign self, looking out for itself, answerable to no one. Scripture’s one is the opposite—the one God who binds His people into one body, and the one flesh that dies to self for the sake of the other.

A subtler corruption dissolves oneness into a vague spiritual “all is one” (monism), erasing the Creator-creature distinction. The Shema resists both errors: God is one, and He is other than His creation, calling a distinct people into covenant union with Himself.
roots_summary: From Old English an and the Hebrew echad—a oneness that can embrace plurality (one flesh from two, one God in three Persons) without ceasing to be one.
roots_lines: Old English an — single, the first cardinal.
Hebrew echad — one; a unity that can comprehend plurality (Genesis 2:24, ‘one flesh’).
Hebrew yachid — the only, solitary one; notably NOT the word chosen for God in the Shema.
Greek heis — one; Paul’s drumbeat in Ephesians 4: one body, one Spirit, one Lord.
usage: The Shema’s “the LORD is one” is the ground of all monotheism and the death of every idol.
In making the two “one flesh,” God stamps marriage with His own covenant faithfulness.
Christ’s prayer that we be one is not a call to bland uniformity but to Spirit-wrought communion.

etymology: Old English twa; the cardinal of pairing. In Scripture the number of witness, agreement, and the covenant strength of the bound pair.
biblical_def: Two is the number of witness and of covenant partnership. By the Law, a matter is established “at the mouth of two or three witnesses”—a single voice cannot condemn; truth must be confirmed. Christ sends the disciples out two by two, and sets the same rule over church discipline: “take with you one or two more, that every word may be established.” Two is also the number of covenant strength against isolation: “two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor”; “can two walk together, unless they are agreed?” The pairing is not mere addition but agreement, mutual help, shared burden. Even the first marriage is God joining two into one flesh, so that two names the strength that comes when the solitary is bound to another in covenant. Yet two can also mark division—two masters, two ways, two houses—for a pair may agree or be set against each other. The number therefore calls for the right second: the witness who confirms the truth, the companion who lifts the fallen, the covenant partner walking in agreement toward one end.
webster_summary: The number of witness and covenant partnership: two or three witnesses establish a matter; two are better than one; but two may also name the division of two ways and two masters.
webster_full: TWO, adj. One more than one; the first plural. In Scripture the number of established witness—no fact condemned on a single testimony—and of the strength of the bound pair over the solitary self.

TWO, n. The pair in covenant agreement (two walking together, two better than one) or in opposition (two masters, two ways). The number asks not merely for a second but for the right second: a true witness, a faithful companion.
scriptures: Ecclesiastes 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
Amos 3:3
Can two walk together, except they be agreed?
Deuteronomy 19:15

One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sinneth: at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established.
Matthew 18:16
But if he will not hear thee, then take with thee one or two more, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.
corruption_summary: The age keeps the pairing but strips the covenant—celebrating partnership without agreement, and reducing the two-witness rule to a technicality rather than God’s guard on truth.
corruption_paragraphs: One corruption prizes companionship without covenant—two walking together who are not agreed, a partnership of convenience that Amos already exposed as impossible in any lasting sense. Biblical two-ness is agreement unto a shared end, not mere proximity.

Another corruption dismisses the two-witness rule as legalism, forgetting that God gave it to protect the accused: no man is to be ruined on a single, unconfirmed voice. The requirement of two is mercy and truth together—a hedge against slander and the lynch mob alike.
roots_summary: From Old English twa and Hebrew shnayim; the biblical weight falls on witness (Hebrew ed) and agreement.
roots_lines: Old English twa — two, the first plural.
Hebrew shnayim — two, a pair.
Hebrew ed — witness; the reason two matters in the Law’s courts.
Greek duo — two; the pattern of the sent pair in the Gospels.
usage: The two-or-three-witness rule shields the innocent as much as it convicts the guilty.
“Two are better than one” commends covenant partnership over the myth of the self-made man.
Amos’s question—“can two walk together, unless they are agreed?”—makes agreement, not mere company, the heart of biblical two-ness.

etymology: Old English siex; the cardinal one short of seven. In Scripture the number of man and his labor—made on the sixth day, set to work six days—and, tripled, the number of man in his rebellion.
biblical_def: Six is the number of man and of labor under the sun. Man was made on the sixth day, and to man the fourth commandment says, “six days you shall labor and do all your work,” before the seventh-day rest. Six is thus the working number, the number of the creature at his appointed task—good, God-given, but not the goal; it always looks toward the seventh, the Sabbath completion it cannot reach on its own. Because it falls one short of seven’s fullness, six can also signify man striving to be complete apart from God, and so becomes the number of rebellion when it is tripled. The mark of the beast is “the number of a man,” six hundred sixty-six—man exalting himself in a mock trinity, forever falling short of the seven of God. Rightly read, six humbles: it sets man in his creaturely place as a worker who must rest in God, not a god who never rests. The sixth-day creature is crowned only when he keeps the seventh-day Sabbath of his Maker.
webster_summary: The number of man and his labor—created on the sixth day, set to six days’ work—and, tripled to 666, the number of man in proud rebellion, ever one short of the seven of God.
webster_full: SIX, adj. One more than five; one less than seven. In Scripture the number of man, made on the sixth day, and of labor, the six working days that precede the Sabbath.

SIX, n. The creature’s number: good in its place, yet always short of seven’s completion. Tripled in Revelation’s 666, it marks man’s self-exaltation—“the number of a man”—a counterfeit fullness that never arrives at the rest of God.

corruption_summary: Modern readings either strip 666 of its meaning (a mere spooky trope) or hunt it as an occult code—both missing that six is simply the number of man, good in labor yet fallen in pride.
corruption_paragraphs: Popular culture reduces 666 to horror-movie décor, a number to shudder at, disconnected from Revelation’s actual point—that it is “the number of a man,” humanity organized against God. The dread is superstition; the meaning is doctrine.

The occult corruption runs the other way, calculating names for the beast as though the text were a cipher to crack. Scripture gives six a plain sense—man and his labor, and man in rebellion—that needs discernment, not decoding.
roots_summary: From Old English siex and Hebrew shesh; the theology comes from the sixth day of creation and the six days of labor, not from number-magic.
roots_lines: Old English siex — six.
Hebrew shesh — six; the day man was made and the span of his labor.
Greek hex — six; behind hexakosioi in the 666 of Revelation.
Pattern: six (man/labor) → seven (God/rest) — the creature crowned only in Sabbath.
usage: Six days of labor are dignified work, but they are ordered toward the seventh-day rest they cannot supply.
The 666 is “the number of a man”—humanity in a mock trinity, ever falling short of the seven of God.
To call six the number of man is to humble him: a worker made to rest in his Maker, not a maker who never rests.

etymology: Old English eahta; the cardinal after seven—the first day of a new week. In Scripture the number of new beginning, covenant sign, and resurrection.
biblical_def: Eight is the number of new beginning. Coming just past seven’s completion, it is the first day of a new week, the start of a new order. On the eighth day the Hebrew son was circumcised—the covenant sign cut into the flesh at the threshold of new life. Eight souls were carried through the flood in the ark, a remnant preserved to begin the world again. And supremely, Christ rose on the first day of the week—the eighth day—inaugurating the new creation; the church has ever called the Lord’s Day the eighth day, the day of resurrection and of the world made new. Eight therefore speaks of what God does after the old order has run its course: circumcision after seven days, salvation through water into a new world, resurrection on the day beyond the Sabbath. It is the number of hope on the far side of completion—not merely rest attained, but life begun again. Where six is man’s labor and seven is God’s rest, eight is the resurrection morning: “It is done—behold, I make all things new.”
webster_summary: The number of new beginning: circumcision on the eighth day, eight souls saved through the flood, and Christ’s resurrection on the eighth day—the first day of the new creation.
webster_full: EIGHT, adj. One more than seven; the first day of a new week. In Scripture the number of new beginning—the eighth day of circumcision, the eighth soul, the day of resurrection.

EIGHT, n. The resurrection number: past the seventh-day rest lies the eighth-day new creation. Christ rose on the first day of the week, and the church keeps that Lord’s Day as the eighth day, the dawn of the world made new.

corruption_summary: The rich biblical meaning of eight—new creation and resurrection—is largely forgotten, flattened into a mere number or swept into occult “lucky eight” superstition.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief corruption is simple neglect: the church has often lost the ancient reading of the eighth day as resurrection and new creation, so that Sunday becomes a bare “day off” rather than the eighth-day dawn of the world made new.

Where meaning is sought, it is often the wrong kind—“lucky eight” in various superstitions, number-magic that promises fortune. Biblical eight promises something far greater and wholly unmagical: resurrection life on the far side of the grave.
roots_summary: From Old English eahta and Hebrew shemonah; the theology flows from the eighth-day covenant sign and the resurrection morning, not from number-magic.
roots_lines: Old English eahta — eight.
Hebrew shemonah — eight; the day of circumcision, the covenant sign in the flesh.
Greek okto — eight; ‘eight souls’ saved through the flood (1 Peter 3:20).
Pattern: seven (rest) → eight (new creation) — the Lord’s Day as resurrection morning.
usage: Circumcision on the eighth day set the covenant sign at the threshold of new life.
The early church called Sunday the eighth day—the day of resurrection and new creation.
Eight souls through the flood were a remnant kept to begin the world again.
